69.t: Rose praises the tunes; Perdido written on a train
69.s: Rose praises Gypsy Without a Song and Lost in Meditation, and Tizol says Perdido was written on a coach seat and handed to Duke.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: You know, "Perdido" was written on the train, on a coach train. I wrote "Perdido" and "Jeffries" was next to me in the seat in the coach, and I started singing this thing to him and he started singing it, too, and I gave it to Duke.

69.s: Barney Bigard mentioned a street named Perdido; since it sounded Spanish for 'lost', Tizol used it.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: Barney told me to call him, because I asked Barney about what's the place of the street where "Some kind of street called the sporting class live, and he said, 'Perdito', 'some kind of street named that."

69.s: Bakiff is published by Tempo and was named by Duke; Tizol does not know what the word means.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: Oh, Bakkeef, that's on Temple. Duke named that tune, called Bakriff, which I don't know what it means -- something about Mecca, I don't know.

69.t: Perdido credits: Persons, Drake, Lenk and Mills
69.s: Tizol does not know Persons or Lenk; Ervin Drake wrote the lyrics and Mills was not on Perdido, which was on Tempo.
69.q: Well, I don't know. In the beginning, at first, there were two people there on the lyrics. Well, later on, I understand it was only Drake.

69.t: Have a Heart and Lost in Meditation: titles change
69.s: Have a Heart is the original title of Lost in Meditation; publishers or Duke changed titles to fit lyrics.

69.t: How Lost in Meditation was written; lyricist Lou Singer
69.s: All his tunes were played on trombone at home, notated and shown to Duke; Lou Singer was a Mills piano-part man.
69.q: Well, the same way. All my tunes, I used to always let Duke hear, you know? Since I was in the band and he was recording pretty near, to be thankful that he would record them, and so I would play them for him and if he liked it, he'd arrange and record it.

69.s: Night Song was credited to Tizol and Mundy and recorded by Charlie Barnet.
69.q: I don't know if Duke arranged that tune or what.

81.t: How he and Fats wrote together; music over lyrics
81.s: Fats would play a tune and Johnson wrote lyrics fast; he preferred writing tunes but was thrown into writing lyrics too.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: Well, see, Fats would play something if he had it, if he had a tune, he'd say, 'Dig this!' and he'd play the tune. Well, you got to be fast enough to write the lyrics.

81.s: Razaf was the first person he collaborated with, a very talented lyricist whose many joint songs were never published.
81.q: Well, Andy Razaf, I would say, you couldn't get a more talented person than Andy Razaf, because he wrote the song, "Ain't Misbehaving", "Honeysuckle Rose", "Supposing" and oh, so many other songs. Later on. But during his tenure and mine, we wrote an awful lot of songs together, songs that were…

81.t: How a composer works: melody like a cyclone
81.s: A tune builds up and comes out of his fingers; he does not labor or rewrite, and never wakes in the night with a song.
81.q: Right. Only think I rewrite are a few poems in that darn book there. I look at them sometimes and I say, 'Oh, that shouldn't be like that' and I make a correction here - and that's about the only thing.

81.s: Neither man had been to Louisiana when they wrote the song, and Johnson calls Razaf prolific and brilliant.
81.ch: Taped excerpts: friends, family and facts
81.q: Just wrote it (inaudible) and I wrote it, And I (inaudible). Nothing unusual about writing a song in those days. You wrote them or you didn't write them.

81.t: Writing both words and music; Cole Porter and Irving Berlin
81.s: Few writers do both; Johnson names Cole Porter and Irving Berlin and plays down his own lyrics.
81.ch: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
81.q: I grew up to it, that's all. I (inaudible) some of the rottenest words in the world and (inaudible). Just because I wrote it doesn't mean it's any good. Yeah, well, --

81.t: Nat Schwartz joins Whiting and Johnson as a trio
81.s: Whiting brought in Nat Schwartz as lyricist; Johnson insisted on credit only for the music.
81.q: So if you'll notice, on any of the songs that are published, you'll see George Whiting and Nat Schwartz, lyric, and music -- J.C. Johnson. See, we got that straight from the beginning; I said, 'Now, I have nothing to do with the lyrics, I'm the tune writer. So I only want credit for what I do,…

589.t: Composing as slowed-down performing; Billy Taylor's memorial
589.s: Lewis explains how composing differs from performing and recalls speaking at Taylor's memorial service.
589.q: now, composition is an important part of my musical life, maybe, I was about to say, equal to – but maybe even equal to performing, because composing, in certain instances, is performing slowed down. You think of these ideas. When you’re performing, they come and go like that, and it’s gone. Either…

589.t: Muses and Amusements with the Turtle Island Quartet
589.s: For a Ravinia bill with Dave Brubeck, Lewis wrote a trio and string quartet piece and learned to let spirit rather than intellect lead.
589.q: My goodness. That’s true. I was invited to – by Welz Kauffman again – to perform a work of my own on the same bill with Dave Brubeck, who chose to write some music for big band. So, when I knew that he was going to do big band, I figured I didn’t

589.t: Jesse Stone and composing with keyboards
589.s: Prompted by Brown's story of Jesse Stone's computer studio, Lewis says he is a manual composer who admires keyboard users.
589.q: Yeah, that’s the way those keyboards came into being, that they were originally made for composers to hear what strings sound like, to hear what this sounds like. They became – the rock-and-roll guys took them and said, oh, I don’t have to go to school. I can just make a trumpet sound like this. I…

589.t: Naming Colors: the Ecology of Oneness
589.s: Colors grew from talks with Guthrie Ramsey, John Hart, and Jan about oneness, with Ramsey coining the title.
589.q: The Evolution of – Colors: the Evolution [sic: Ecology] of Oneness – actually, Guthrie Ramsey came up with the name after I had been talking with Michael [?Kochs], who is an artist-designer in his own right, with his own company, who works with me sometimes. He – Michael – had asked me, what’s…

589.t: Jan helps him write the ballet To Know Her Is to Love Her
589.s: Stuck writing music for the Joffrey ballet, he follows Jan's advice to record himself playing freely, producing the eight-piece suite.
589.q: The lady Jan, my wife, is meaningful to me in many ways. Not only does she remind me – now it’s become a habit. I always like vegetables anyway – “Eat your vegetables.” She’s a health – “When are you going to go down to the treadmill? You didn’t go yesterday.” She’s so wonderful, and we share so…

950.t: Composing the Creole song 'Who told you I was going there?'
950.s: He explains how a remark by Picou's brother led him to compose a Creole song about two friends arguing.
950.q: Yeah, well that's what I'm coming to. And he said, I'll have to translate it for you because he said it in Creole. It means, who told you I was going there? I told him nobody said you was going there. I told him in French, nobody was going there. And from that, I just started and started to play…

950.t: Reviving 'Down in the Tin Cup Room' and other old tunes
950.s: He describes unwritten old tunes he heard at picnics and in the red-light district, which he plans to rework and write down.
950.q: Some of the words. Yeah, and they used to sing around the red light district and so forth. But I figured on revising it and using it, not in that way, but using the idea. Down in the Tin Cup Room where I used to go, when they knocked me to the floor and took all my dough. I'm going to fix it up…

950.t: His original 'A La Ba' and getting his compositions recorded
950.s: He distinguishes his original La Ba, composed about 1910-14, from other versions and asks for help to copyright and record it.
950.q: They're real good. They're real good. And in fact, if a person doesn't understand the Creole, of course it jives better when you hear the Creole and can understand it. I suppose, yeah. Because there's two fellows. And they actually, it seemed as though there was something that the two of them was…

950.t: Piron's first composition and the song 'What is this world to me'
950.s: He recalls meeting Piron at Bloom's, and arranging Piron's first composition with Freddie Ratlin's words around 1911-12.
950.q: Piron. I met Piron out at Blooms. I'm telling you, with the office, I'm telling you about at Blooms. He played in the office and so forth. He became good friends, musicians, and so forth. And when he had a barbie shop there on Cravon Street near Columbus, right near Stewart was where the Musicians…

717.t: Writing longhand at home, not using Finale
717.s: Abene writes longhand in a basement office and jokes about Finale.
717.q: Yeah. I have an office down in the basement, converted, and that where both my and my wife’s office area is. And I don’t even write — I have a really nice Steinway grand upstairs in the living room which I hardly use. I use a Technics basic piano sound to write on, downstairs. And I write in…

717.s: He begins pieces with rhythms, then melody and harmony, capturing ideas on scratch paper and keeping alternates.
717.q: Well it happens both ways. Sometimes they will give you a specific — now say I want you to write a piece for trombone, or I want you to write a piece to feature it. Now one piece I’m working on now for the Metropole Orchestra again in the Netherlands is to feature their brass section. It’s a…

717.s: Abene finds titles hard, and discusses Braxton's schematics and his own piece titles.
717.q: That’s a great question. Yeah I have a major problem sometimes thinking of titles. Sometimes I’ll be sitting there and like I’ll have a list of some titles I’m trying to call this brass piece. And I’m thinking oh man I’ll finish the chart and I won’t have a title. That’s my biggest worry. I’ll say…

717.t: Several pieces at once, deadlines and teaching schedule
717.s: Abene works on two or three pieces at once and works best near the deadline, citing the seven-trombone piece for the Metropole Orchestra; he teaches four days a week and co-directs the BMI workshop.
717.q: It’s a very good question. It’s variable. It all depends. Some pieces fall into place a little easier. It’s hard. Sometimes I’ve had more trouble figuring what to do with a band than I do with a full orchestra. Or vice versa. There’s no set thing for me on it. And I’m generally working on two or…

966.t: What makes a tune memorable; learning accessibility from Bob Mintzer
966.s: Rowe asks how Davis would sing the melody; Davis says he and Cole favor accessibility, learned from years in Bob Mintzer's band.
966.ch: Open City and the economics of records
966.q: I mean I could, in a really horrific way sing the melody that Cole wrote, but yeah I think I would probably say that I — in my own writing and I think Cole does the same thing — we really like to have some level of accessibility to it so that it feels like, you know, what you just described, and I…

966.s: Davis describes melody-, harmony- and rhythm-first composing approaches.
966.q: I’m not sure where it starts. I mean I think there’s a couple different approaches that I use and one is melody based, you know where the first thing that you come up with is a melody that anybody could — you just have something in your head and it could be a fragment of something else you’d heard…

966.t: Bob Mintzer's advice to title a piece first
966.s: Davis recalls composition lessons with Mintzer and his advice to title a song before writing.
966.q: Bob Mintzer told me once, I took some lessons from him before I was in his band, for composition and arranging. And Bob said, “You know before you start it title your song.” And it was really an interesting thought. I don’t always do it, sometimes I do it after it’s done and has a vibe that I think…

966.s: Davis explains the 9/11 memorial for six trombones and the Oakland A's mascot tune, and how titles shape music.
966.q: melody in on top of that. And then kind of the third way would be dealing with the rhythmic element first and that’s going to create a different approach to how you’re going to write the melody. So I think I just kind of roll with whatever happens on that. The two tunes that you are referencing,…

466.s: Asked if he was commissioned by a baseball team, he explains the Dodgers asked him to write the song, recorded with Alan Broadbent and Sue Raney.
466.q: Yeah. I mean they asked me if I wouldn’t mind writing it. I mean they kind of invited me to write it. And it’s “Dodger Blue” you’re speaking of. Yeah. But there was no commission involved really. That’s too nice a word for it. It was really, they were nice

466.s: He credits Bob Dorough as the heart of Schoolhouse Rock and discusses their collaborations 'I'm Hip' and 'Who's on First'.
466.q: That was Bob Dorough’s baby. Somebody thought the idea up but Dorough contributed the musical thing. He was the musical director and it was the stamp of Bob Dorough that made that show what it was. That and the great artwork. Dorough is a particular hero of mine.

466.t: How long a lyric takes: 'Blizzard of Lies' and 'Hershey Bar'
466.s: A title can wait years; on deadline for Johnny Mandel he took four days, three of nothing, and finds pressure stimulating.
466.q: That one took years. Not because it took years, because I carried the title around in my head for years before I ever acted on it. But I remember thinking that would be a great title. And then I never really followed through on it. I had it in mind for a decade though. But otherwise it depends. If…

466.t: Songwriting craft: titles, puzzles and topical songs
466.s: Lyrics are like crossword puzzles; he starts from a title, and dislikes writing topical material.
466.q: Well I think just about all songs are that way. I’ve often thought of them as that way. Always it’s very much like a crossword puzzle of some kind, yeah.

472.t: Melodize, composing over the years, and using Finale
472.s: Rowe congratulates Heath on his career and book; they discuss the word 'melodize', how his composing has improved, and how Apple computers and Finale help him prepare music.
472.q: Yeah, well melodize. I’ve heard that word before from others. So I don’t know where it came from but it floats around so anybody can use it, as you said you did.

472.s: Heath explains how he uses the computer and notation software and gets ideas at the piano and saxophone, as Dizzy advised.
472.q: I use a computer for everything now, except to get ideas together. To format everything I’ve been on the computer since I started teaching at Queens, ’86 or ’87, that’s when I got my first computer and got my first notation program. Now it’s really advanced, a program called Finale. Well, I get…

472.t: Counting his compositions and writing by machine versus live players
472.s: Heath tallies his compositions and extended works, including 'Three Ears', and discusses the computer's limits.
472.q: Yes I have, it’s a hundred and some. All of this is in my book because I had the extended works. The last long piece, extended piece, was written for the Ciano Jazz Repertorio. It’s supposed to be released this year. About a year or so ago, two years maybe, I wrote this piece called “The Endless…

472.t: Music in the sky and the search for originality
472.s: Heath says music is there for everyone to grab and that finding originality is hard.
472.q: Yeah, because I’ve had some T-Shirts made last year that said, “Music is in the sky for everyone to grab some,” because we get hung up on one person, the American media gets hung up: Coltrane, Miles, Bo, Bump, whoever. But it’s a lot of people [who] got music, and a lot of people can get it. That’s…

580.t: Concerto Peligroso and holding back the bass and drums
580.s: Rowe praises the changing textures of Israels' piece; Israels explains delaying the bass-and-drums time feel for effect.
580.q: Of course. Yeah. Well I thought the bass and drums playing time feels so good but it feels better if it comes as the lagniappe at the end you know? And when I listen to that I think maybe I held it back a little too long, I’m not sure in terms of the proportions and balance and that. But boy when…

580.t: Inspiration from other people's music: Skipping Tune and Walkin' Up
580.s: Israels says composing starts from others' music and explains how Skipping Tune derives from Bill Evans' piece, with a brief audio dropout.
580.q: Well I wrote a piece called “Skipping Tune.” It’s my version of Bill Evans’ piece called “Walking Up.” It is built of the same mat — no, he made a piece out of these kinds of materials, exclusively these kinds of materials. Major 7 chords, minor 7 chords and no dominants. But he did it in such a…

580.t: Photograph not painting, and the polyester leisure suit piece
580.s: Israels says his music comes from musical ideas, not pictures, and tells of a 1970s Maiden Voyage-influenced piece he dislikes but just recorded.
580.q: me do my own version of that. So my pieces are, they come from other musical ideas that I’ve heard. And that’s just me. I don’t care if you want to write a piece about if you’re Charles Ives and you want to write the Housatonic at Stockbridge I know Stockbridge and the Housatonic River very well…

580.s: Israels says titles come arbitrarily, sometimes before the piece; Rowe mentions Braxton's diagram titles.
580.q: Sometimes before the piece, sometimes there’s a list of them and I just stick one on. Because they mostly, it’s pretty hard to describe. It could be Composition #1, Composition #3, Composition #47 so the answer is they come kind of arbitrarily. I’ve got to give it a name.

942.t: How she would approach a commission
942.s: Asked what she would ask a commissioner, she says she would learn about the person's place and culture, like a painting commission.
942.q: I think, whoa that’s a big one. I’m certainly not going to dump my world onto yours and go I’m just going to do this. I would want to get to know a little bit about the space you’re living in and what is feeding your environment culturally and through the natural and through the urban environment…

942.t: Titles as memory, the present moment and fantasy; literature
942.s: She says her instrumental pieces reflect childhood memories, the present moment (paddleboarding) or imagination, and mentions her love of American literature such as Jonathan Franzen.
942.q: So sometimes I guess I do reflections and sometimes I’m doing — or reflections from childhood and other times I’m doing reflections of something very recent. Or I might be imagining something I’ve never done so there’s no rhyme or reason to titles sometimes. But fantasy is a big part of it for me.…

942.t: Writing by hand and the need for a home studio
942.s: She sketches on a notepad and uses the computer only for large ensemble scores; compares Dave Rivello's workspace and her Montreal studio.
942.q: No. I wish. I can barely turn my computer on when I’m composing. Once I get into it I will, and that means writing larger ensemble music. I can write all small sketches on a notepad. That’s what I do. Yeah.

942.t: Obsessing over a composition; episodic writing as puzzle
942.s: The drums and bass are briefly debated, then she describes composing as problem solving, episodic and like a puzzle.
942.q: Yeah it’s the construction that goes on and you’re, again this interview I did before had a similar question and I was just like — he asked me, he said, “So do you ever dream about your compositions? Like do you have dreams about compositions or that you want to have?” And I was like you mean…

502.s: He writes changes first, then melody and lyrics, avoids standard forms, and explains that he does not chase trends but aims to create a timeless body of work.
502.q: Well I have the computer but I usually do that post-writing. No I just kind of sit there and play piano until I get a series, a progression or a series of changes that intrigues me. Usually the changes come first and then I’ll write the melody and the lyrics.

502.t: Choosing songs and writing lyrics to Man from Tanganyika
502.s: Songs intrigue him by their changes or intervals; he researched Tanganyika to write lyrics to McCoy Tyner's tune, paying respect to African influence.
502.q: It’s just those things and intrigue me, yeah, that either they sink into my head and I can’t get them out of my head, or they’re so just intriguing, either the changes or the intervals or whatever in the melody, like McCoy’s “Man from Tanganyika” was in twelve-eight and it had these bars of…

502.t: Lyric writing: Count to Two and Taken to Heart
502.s: He discusses clichés and double entendre, the origin of Count to Two in Eddie Gomez's remark, writing a verse on a plane, and disliking perfunctory bebop lyrics.
502.q: You know I don’t know. Trying not to — I don’t want to use clichés as clichés, but I love to take clichés — I love double entendre. My second album was entitled “Double Entendre.” So that’s how much I love them. So I try to just put a little twist on things and maybe turn it around or juxtapose…

502.s: Rowe calls him an arranger; they discuss medleys on his CDs and how quoting tunes came with experience.
502.q: Yeah, you know I talk to Kenny Werner, a great piano player, and he would always quote other tunes in the middle of his solos, you know, a lot of players do that.

511.t: Writing 'Widow's Walk', the first track of his first record
511.s: Rowe recalls hearing the tune on radio; Margitza says it came in half an hour, built from an ostinato and bass line at the piano.
511.q: Thank you. Yes I do, because certain songs come out really quickly and others take a while to work through and for whatever reason it just happens like that and one is not necessarily better than the other but “Widow’s Walk” literally came out in about a half an hour. It’s one of those that came…

511.s: Titles can be harder than songs; he explains the widow's walk image.
511.q: I actually don’t remember. You know sometimes, I don’t know if it’s the same for you, actually finding the title for the song is harder than writing the song.

511.t: Practicing and composing in his head; Schoenberg's walks
511.s: He practices ideas in all keys mentally, citing Jerry Bergonzi and Schoenberg, who composed away from the piano.
511.q: Yes. Actually I have —I shouldn’t say developed the ability over the years, it’s just something that has happened is, even without, even like aside from composing is that I will practice in my head. There was recently an interesting little — I think it was one of those things called profiles in…

511.t: Composing away from the piano; influence versus plagiarism
511.s: He tries starting from sax, groove or movies instead of piano, and they trade quotes on influence (Pepper Adams).
511.q: Well not complet — I mean I kind of came up with this little descending line and then I tinkered with it. So when I improvised it it wasn’t in its final form but I just kind of came up with that melody as a result of hearing the ostinato in the chords. And I mean these days there’s a — I think it’s…

750.t: Her first songs: 'All the Pretty Bubbles' and an angry song in 1971
750.s: She wrote a song about bubbles at four; her first real song came in 1971 from anger at her second husband.
750.q: No not at all. But it was very interesting. It was very interesting structure. It went [sings] all the pretty bubbles I see/ all the pretty bubbles I see/all the pretty bubbles I see — and you know it kept going up, like the bubbles.

750.t: Songs that write themselves and writing to criteria
750.s: Her best songs seem to write themselves; she describes writing a Saffire Christmas song and says subject matter is the hard part.
750.ch: Songwriting craft and the blues form
750.q: I don’t know. Well I think I’ve heard fiction writers talk about this too. I mean I suppose I could have wrestled, I was talking about writing an intro to a song, ‘cause like all that classic blues stuff, doing that Bessie Smith and the Ma Rainey and all that stuff it’s got those little…

750.t: Blues limitations, major sevenths and Bruce Iglauer
750.s: Blues is open and limited like haiku; she snuck in a major seventh despite Iglauer's rule, and limits give a different kind of freedom.
750.ch: Songwriting craft and the blues form
750.q: It’s very, very open. And people, of course I write stuff that’s not that A-A-B form all the time. But people say, “How can you write blues?” My jazz friends say, “Oh it’s so dull, it’s so limited.” And I say, “Are you familiar with Haiku?”

750.t: Writing a song in her head, a stolen bass lick and listening widely
750.s: She composes mentally, writing about not being sad enough for blues, and borrowed a lick from a Texas bass player.
750.q: No. I can do that in my head. I mean it’s good later on I get to a piano. But I can — night before last there was a song that I do that I was going to try a different rhythm and different pattern with the piano on it. And I lay around and did it in my head. I mean I

722.t: Writing on King brand manuscript paper
722.s: Rivello writes scores longhand and explains his stockpile of King brand paper once used by Brookmeyer and Gil Evans.
722.q: Yeah, it’s part of the process for me and so the computer has its things and in many ways it’s made life easier as a composer and arranger, but for me, I still am — I have to work on paper. And so I write all my scores longhand, I do all my sketching and my full scores longhand, and then put it…

722.t: How much he hears in his head and gambling in composition
722.s: He has written since junior high; he gambles when writing for his own band, as Brookmeyer, Schneider and Holman also did.
722.q: I’ve been writing music since I was in junior high school, not that anybody should ever hear those attempts at that point, but it’s been a lot of years. So it’s a two part answer I guess. I can hear a lot of things in my head. And if I were to write something very

722.t: Sketches on the piano and solving problems away from it
722.s: He explains his current sketches, including a piece for Peter Erskine, and says he works on one piece at a time.
722.q: No. There is, sort of. But they don’t all fit together. Each one is in some way some other piece that might someday come into existence. So this is something that just happened one night. It’s not really that good yet, but it could be something. And this and the things here I’m now in the process…

722.s: He keeps lists of titles; his titles have meaning but the music is not programmatic.
722.q: All the time. And I keep lists of things that seem good. And that helps sometimes, and sometimes it’s pretty hysterical when you go back to that list and it’s like really? I

408.t: How he composes and his view of electronics
408.s: Woods writes from practice notes, then at keyboard and computer, and says he is done experimenting with electronics.
408.q: No. I sketch maybe. No I usually write at the couch. Usually when I’m practicing I’ll come across something I like and I have a lot of little notes and stuff. Little patterns or something that I find intriguing. And then I’ll take that to the keyboard and see where we can go harmonically with it, I…

408.t: Computer notation: Music Printer Plus and Sibelius
408.s: His move to notation software and the rondo joke.
408.q: I had the very, very first Music Printer Plus, which was the first music program; it was an old DOS based program, yeah. Because I got tired of having my sketches on the back of matchbook covers, and a piece of paper here. Now I have all of my music is in the computer, everything I’ve ever written…

408.s: Technology helps him send parts around the world.
408.q: Exactly. Well, I remember sending some--, when I used to write it by hand, I remember sending arrangements to Spain and they got lost in the mail. And I was writing the music at the computer. But my son says, Hey, Pop, you know you can send it by pdf.” I said, “PD What?” And he said, come here, you…

408.s: Jotting ideas, gestation, and odd bar counts.
408.q: apropos of nothing but … nevertheless, when I look like I’m not doing anything, I’m thinking about, I think about songs. I wake up in the middle of the night just like in the movies, I dash to the --, I carry a little booklet with me, you know, with staffs, and I jot down ideas and stuff. But, I…

141.t: Developing the left hand and how songs got written
141.s: He worked on technique alone and had no deadlines; Audre says he taped songs for the label.
141.q: I remember when you started really concentrating on developing your left hand as well as your right hand. That was a kind of major change.

141.t: Left hand practice and songs that just appeared
141.s: Audre does not recall him writing the songs; they simply appeared.
141.q: Yeah. That’s the only time I remember you talking about concentrating, some reasons why you wanted to develop the left hand... Up to that point... Of course, I was busy. But I don’t remember your writing songs. I don’t remember where it all happened, even. It must have been while I was at work.

141.t: Where Wild Man On The Loose came from
141.s: He got the idea from a man just in from the country, not a particular friend.
141.q: I got the idea for that...I was playing at Sugar Hill in ‘60. I think it was after ‘60... But

141.t: My Back Yard and Your Mind Is On Vacation
141.s: Audre links My Back Yard to his meditative sitting; Your Mind Is On Vacation came from talkers at the Showboat.
141.q: Well, this one, “My Back Yard,” Mose used to, at some time during every day, sit in the back yard. I called him “Little Buddha.”

470.t: The German radio question and the 22nd Psalm cantata

470.t: Writing on commission and choosing texts: the Bible, Mari Evans and Dunbar
470.s: Baker prefers commissions with set parameters and chooses texts mainly from the Bible, Mari Evans and Paul Laurence Dunbar, including works for the Fisk Jubilee Singers.
470.ch: His own groups, compositions and friends
470.q: I think that’s a normal procedure with commissioning. Basically, the more parameters prescribed by the commissioner, the easier it is to write the piece. When you tell me it’s for – it’s this many minutes long, now you’ve already made that a little easier. You tell me it’s going to be three…

470.t: Calling the muse: advice from teachers
470.s: Baker recommends Koestler and Nachmanovitch, recounts writing Kosbro in an auditorium, Donald Erb's daily writing hours, and the difference between a song and a theme.
470.ch: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
470.q: Basically, for me, I go to a lot of sources. Part of it is intuition. Part of it is experiential knowledge. But there are some books I would recommend to anybody. One is The Act of Creation, which is a marvelous book. It’s by the guy who wrote the book Darkness at Noon, Arthur Koestler –…

470.t: Testing a theme and word play
470.s: He turns a theme upside down and sideways to test whether it can bear fruit, and uses puns and word play as exercises in changing context.
470.ch: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
470.q: Copyright infringement. So I try to devise all the techniques – and, you know, it’s another reason why I engage in so much word play, because with word play, what you’re doing is taking any particular idea and putting it in as many different settings as possible. I get into puns and into word play,…

65.s: Mambo a la Savoy with Walter Fuller and others; he estimates over 150 tunes.

65.q: Ahh, "Mambo a la Savoy" with Walter Fuller. "Yo tengo un ate", "Te lo dije my Friend", "I like the Puerto Rican Way" and -----

And said: "oh, come on Machito, maybe you lose the touch because you've been in the United States for so long that now you consider anybody you…

65.q: Well, 'La Paella'. That was Federico that asked me if I ever tried Paella, you know, the Spanish dish. I said: Oh, come on Federico, I even know how to make it.

65.ch: Rising in Manhattan: clubs, Hilda and the Latin scene
65.q: Oh!! "Sopa de Pichon" - because, you know, there was ahh an atmosphere, happy atmosphere, and about - have a good time, forget it - and they called that particular happy cigarette. "Pichon"........

454.t: Throwing drafts away, unfinished songs and Fables of Faubus lyrics
454.s: Composing frees him from interference; words slow his songs; Faubus words came after the music.
454.ch: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
454.q: If I got a piece -- I got some I haven't even finished. I got one, (singing), take any choice from one to ten, bet you I've got your number, you're still in love with me. I always wanted to finish that one and I never have. Probably because the words don't -- that is it, it's because the words…

454.t: Spontaneous composition, piano fingering and throwing music away
454.s: His own piano fingering system, discarding pieces, and notating the six-eight theme of Revelations in four-four.
454.q: comes to my head, and not miss too many notes, I get away with it. On bass -- I'm talking about piano because my schooling was not that hip on piano. It was all my own fingering, most of it. I studied jazz piano with Lloyd Reese, and the scales weren't that hard, the scales. The proper fingering…

454.t: Early compositions of 1943 and having no favorites
454.s: Miss Bliss and other early pieces written in California; his favorite is always the next one.
454.ch: Town Hall, Vanguard and large works
454.q: I don't have any favorites. The one I'm doing next is my favorite.

454.t: Superimposed meters, the Workshop and the operatic ballet idea
454.s: Writing everything out in the Workshop era, plans for an operatic ballet with Katherine Dunham and street voices, and his unrealized ambitions.
454.q: Yeah. That's when I had that superb energy to want to do something like that. Because it wasn't just talk to say -- to do a operatic ballet, with tap dances from the Baby Laurence (inaudible) era. And -- well, in those times, Melissa Hayden from the classical dance era, Katherine Dunham from the…

124.t: Writing "You Showed Me the Way" with Bud Green
124.s: Robbins paired McRae's melody with lyricist Bud Green; credit was shared with Ella and Chick Webb.
124.ch: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40

124.s: McRae recalls working weeks on each song with pianist Una Mae Carlisle, who wrote "Walking by the River"; Welburn adds her death in 1956.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45

124.s: McRae stayed in New York writing for the Robbins staff, including "Santa Rosa" and "I'm Afraid of Love".
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45

I had some other writing to do for Robbins at that time, you know. (Inaudible). Then (inaudible) the things that I…

124.t: Writing rhythm and blues for publishers
124.s: With Sid Wyche, Charlie Singleton and others, McRae composed and arranged songs that publishers placed with artists.

278.t: Novelty songs and writing with artists in the room
278.s: He relates novelty tunes to street humor and describes writing songs with artists present, including It's Raining with Irma Thomas.
278.q: Well, here I can certainly afford to speak of that because he was such a mess that those novelty type tunes. I can see a correlation there. There was a whole era of things like doing the Shirley Ellis days of Banana Banner for Fenn and things like that. And they had a lot of these and Purple People…

278.t: Sansu Enterprises and writing for Lee Dorsey
278.s: With Marshall Sehorn he formed Sansu in 1965; Lee Dorsey's personality inspired songs like Working in the Coal Mine.
278.ch: Sansu, Irma, Lee Dorsey and the Meters
278.q: Lee Dorsey's way of being and his voice has a lot to do with those songs being in existence. None of the Lee Dorsey songs would have been written if it wasn't for Lee. I would say that. Well, in a way the same for Irma Thomas, but there are some songs that I wrote for Irma that sound quite normal…

278.t: The Stokes, Whipped Cream and Java
278.s: Whipped Cream was written for the Stokes as a joke; he had Al Hirt in mind after Java.
278.q: Right. Whipped Cream was written for the Stokes as a joke. We'd do things in the Stokes, even though it was supposed to be a conventional rock band. We would do things like Spike Jonze and we'd rehearse the tune sometime that we had to tear a piece of paper or drop a piece of tin on the floor. So…

196.t: Piron's Purple Rose of Cairo and Leclerc's second part
196.s: Leclerc says he wrote the second part of Piron's Purple Rose of Cairo; they look at sheet music and find Jimmy Dupree wrote the words and Steve Lewis co-wrote it.
196.q: I thought Jimmy Dupree wrote that. Oh no, no, Jimmy Dupree. Wrote the words or something. No. Jimmy Dupree used to write all lyrics. Yeah, lyrics, that's what I mean.

196.t: Henry Therian, Joe Virgis and writing Too Late to Be Sorry Now
196.s: Leclerc, Joe Virgis and Texas singer Henri Therian wrote Too Late to Be Sorry Now; all three names are on the Cameo record.

Joe Voyage just met him. And then the three of us got together and we wrote Too Late to Be Sorry Now. I think he…

196.t: How Someday You Want Me was written
196.s: He wrote it while fooling around at the piano, not in love.
196.ch: Pianists, radio and cafes of old New Orleans
196.q: want me to want you oh I guess one of those things sitting around food around the piano

434.t: Writing lyrics to given titles: Gravy Waltz, Picnic, Tell Me Your Dreams
434.s: Allen explains his different approaches to songwriting and how he wrote lyrics for Ray Brown's Gravy Waltz and the Picnic theme.
434.q: Yes. Of all the ways that you can approach and complete a song, I work in all of them. If there are let’s say ten ways, it doesn’t follow that I do ten percent Way A, ten percent Way B, I don’t think there are any relevant statistics on that, but it depends on what the assignment is. Sometimes I…

434.t: Writing the lyric to South Rampart Street Parade by slowing the record
434.s: Allen tells how he wrote the lyric in 1951 by playing the 78 at 33 1/3, then a time check.
434.q: Rampart Street Parade,” and consequently it is partly martial. The reason I’m laughing now is I dictated that phrase the other day and somebody wrote M-A-R-S-H-A-L-L, as if it was part of the Marshall plan. M-A-R-T-I-A-L folks. Anyway, it was part of the — and if you think of it, the very opening…

434.t: Titling instrumentals and starting from a title
434.s: Allen recalls asking bandleaders how they titled instrumentals, Goodman's reply about Benji, and writing Pretend You Don't See My Heart from a title.
434.q: That also is a marvelous question, that’s what you do for a living, you ask marvelous questions. I jump back to, I don’t know about 40 years ago, I once got intrigued by that question, and I wrote to about 20 band leaders, including Benny. This was long before I’d met him. He had some…

435.t: Composing for goals: the 2004 Lincoln Center commission
435.s: Fingers-first ideas versus commissions, including the Let Freedom Swing piece co-composed with Zim Ngqawana.
435.q: Oh absolutely. There’s — look in terms of waiting for something to happen if I just come up with a phrase when I’m practicing — some things don’t come from the brain, they come from the fingers you know. And it won’t be — in my case — I’m not that brilliant that it will be complete but it will be…

435.t: Starting a piece from a verbal cue
435.s: A trick learned from Dave: take a speech rhythm or phone number and bring it into music.
435.q: So you know I’ll grab something from outside of music and try to bring it into music and then see if that does something.

435.s: Ideas arise away from the piano; he is always processing and can switch off by focusing elsewhere.
435.q: Oh yeah, all the time. I never put — well I shouldn’t say never — I very seldom, if I’m driving by myself I probably won’t put the radio on in the car. On plane rides I only watch the movie if I’m very tired. I’m always processing something, and sometimes that processing is just rumination, it’s…

394.t: Whether to explain original pieces, and the piece 'Unwritten'
394.s: She is of two minds about introducing pieces; 'Unwritten' honours the unwritten stories of women in her lineage.
394.q: That’s a really good question, and I’m always in two minds about it. Because obviously music is – well instrumental music this is obviously wordless stories let’s say. So there is something about allowing the audience to have their own experience of it and make their

394.t: 'Insomnia', Paul Clarvis's feel, and playing alone
394.s: 'Insomnia' was written after a 3 A.M. wake-up; the live version with Paul Clarvis swings; she enjoys solo saxophone.
394.q: Sometimes the titles are literal. Yeah, that was very much – I go through periods of really quite terrible insomnia. And so sometimes I just get up and go and write something. So that was a 3 A.M. wake-up, this is not happening, I don’t want to read a book, I don’t want to meditate, I’m going to go…

394.t: Scores, piano parts and pen-and-paper versus Sibelius
394.s: She writes loose 'ish' sketches and detailed piano voicings, starting on paper and then using Sibelius.
394.q: Ooo. Yeah. Probably. I do write things down most of the time. Sometimes that will be a scribble on a piece of paper and it will sort of say, I use the word “ish” quite a lot. So the B minor-ish, as in eh, we might have a sort of tonic area of B and let me see what happens. And I play with people…

504.t: First compositions, titles and Malibu Reggae
504.s: He writes from piano improvisations, sometimes starting with a title, such as Malibu Reggae for Directions' first ECM album.
504.q: Well you know I think I wrote improvising on the piano, so out of the improvisations would come compositions. Sometimes a composition was written because I had a title before I did the composition. So the composition, the title fit the outcome of the composition.

504.t: Tribute to Erik Satie on the Newvelle solo album
504.s: He explains writing his Satie tribute in 4/4 in F sharp, with a minor ending in homage to Satie.
504.q: Oh you mean from the Newvelle solo, yeah. Yeah no I love Satie, so I just decided to let my intuition write that. So instead of it being in 3/4 like “Gymnopedie” is, I wrote it in 4/4. But I did use some of the, shall we say the things that Satie used in “Gymnopedie.” And it’s like F sharp, which…

504.t: Enjoying challenges and preparing for arranged music
504.s: He likes challenges and prepares from audio and charts; Joanne Brackeen's fast chord changes for Eddie Gomez stretched him.
504.q: Yeah I like the challenges actually. Because it helps you grow and helps you develop. You gain more, like I say, wisdom for jazz, some of the challenging music that you have to play. I had to play I mean.

718.t: Writing on the road with a small battery keyboard
718.s: He wrote in hotel rooms on a small keyboard that let him hear whole voicings.
718.q: No I never really wrote on the bus while it was moving. I would do it in the hotel rooms. I’d do it when he had a break or a day off. I carried a little keyboard about this big, battery powered, that I had in my suitcase, which I still have. And I wrote with, up until about three or four years ago,…

718.t: Writing by hand versus notation software
718.s: Computer notation changed his thought process; he learned it cold turkey on tour and finds playback useful.
718.q: It did for a short time I think. I mean it probably would be inaudible to most people. But it affected the way I write and the thought process. I had to find a way around — strangely enough — I had to find my way around the technology to get to the music. I mean in the past writing with pencil and…

718.s: He asks about a group's talent and limits before writing commissions.
718.q: Yeah I don’t want to say it’s harder. I would say there’s a higher chance — a greater chance that what I do may not fit this person’s group. If they say we don’t care, just write something, and they give me no limitations, I’m going to write for my own band and then give them the chart. They’ll pay…

958.t: How Fleck writes and chooses tunes for the band
958.s: Fleck writes constantly and picks the tune that has an intangible something, either striking simplicity or interesting complexity. He then problem-solves how it fits the group.
958.q: Not so much. Like I just write a lot. And I’m always screwing around with the banjo and stuff pops out and then I try to figure out what’s going to be good for the group. And a lot of times I just take what I think is the best song and what makes it the best song to me is hard to put my finger on…

958.t: Falling in love with your own tunes without fooling yourself
958.s: Fleck wants his writing to be truly beautiful rather than a groove or progression that lulls an audience. He makes his tunes get past his own critical listening.
958.q: I don’t want it to be cheap. I want it to be for real. I want it to really be a beautiful melody and not just people — because you can lull people into that state just by playing a certain groove and a certain type of chord progression and at a gig they’ll go, “oh that was so beautiful” but you…

958.s: The melody came out while Fleck tested microphones for 'Solo Banjo Works', before the Flecktones. The bridge came later and the title from a road sign seen on a bus; the bridge's harmony also surprised him.
958.q: Yeah. I mean I was really happy with it. It popped out. I was recording an album called “Solo Banjo Works” back whenever it was, before the Flecktones. And I was testing the microphones and I just was improvising a little bit and that melody came out and I just kept playing it over and over again.…

559.t: How he composes, from practicing, and early compositions
559.s: He composes from ideas found while practicing, writing for the group; his first piece 'Laughing Guitar' was recorded by Duane Eddy.
559.q: No. Okay, there are two ways to compose that I know. One was what you just mentioned. Doc Pomus and Morty Shuman used to spend six and eight hours a day composing. And I didn’t. I would find stuff while I’m practicing or playing and then I’d start to develop it. And I’d develop it into, it would…

559.t: The origin of 'Barcelona' and Dizzy adopting it
559.s: He tells how his favorite composition grew from open-string voicings, Getz's missed chance, and Dizzy liking the chord.
559.q: Thank you. You know what? That happens to be my favorite composition. And I got only one bad break on it. Stan Getz wanted to record it. And Stan said, “Give me the music, I’ll record it.” So I gave him the music and then two months later he passed away. But I would have loved to have him record it…

559.t: Lead sheets, fake books and 'Barcelona' jam sessions
559.s: He writes lead sheets for publishing; none of his tunes are in fake books, though 'Barcelona' is played at jam sessions.
559.q: Yeah you write a lead sheet with the melody and you write it with the changes above it and that’s really good enough for the publishing part of it, for the Library of Congress it’s good enough, yeah.

328.t: Approaching a commission and writing for players
328.s: He starts from finding a melody, writes by inspiration, and says music begins when players interpret it; bands used to play pieces long before recording.
328.q: Well I’ve been asked the question many times how do you start to approach either a composition or an arrangement. You have to start actually just be getting an idea of what it is that whoever you’re going to do it for, wants. And then to let it develop in a natural way. And the feeling for it, and…

328.t: Transposed scores and writing by hand
328.s: He writes transposed scores in pen or pencil, not on computers.
328.q: Let him do all of that transposition, you know. I think man, boy that must be a job. So I always did develop the transposed score approach. And I also write with a pen or pencil. I don’t use computers or anything like that. I enjoy writing the traditional way.

328.s: Writing by inspiration on Dizzy's themes.
328.ch: Dizzy's legacy, Latin rhythm and closing
328.q: Mainly just writing by inspiration, letting his music direct me wherever I’m going to go with my interpretation of his compositions. Because he was such a great theorist himself, he was so well-trained in harmony and all of that, and he developed such a knowledge of harmony and orchestration, and…

719.s: Hey hears riffs in passing and likes to step away from a track and think about the part.
719.q: It kind of, in passing if I hear something — the other day I heard some vocal riff that was — wow that was really cool. How can we make that, how can I make that into a horn part that works you know. Stuff like that. But if I’m kind of working on a song and I used to like to listen to it, work on…

719.t: Writing horn parts on computer and how notation should look
719.s: Hey uses Logic, set up by his son, for demos and printed parts, and explains how he likes music notated.
719.q: About ten years ago a guy was working on — he wanted to do a Broadway show. And it was kind of on Studio 54 back in the sort of disco days kind of. And he had these songs and he wanted me to send him demos. And I said well I’ve got like 40 years of demos out there. You know what I do. If you want…

719.t: How Hey gets an assignment: cassettes and lead sheets
719.s: Hey has perfect pitch and usually gets only a cassette of the song, listening closely to the whole track before writing.
719.q: Almost in every case all I got was, well back then a cassette. You know Quincy, David Foster or any of these things, they would send me a cassette of the song. That’s it. If I ever got a lead sheet –- which was rare — I never looked at it because by the time the lead sheet — I did it in the…

694.t: What keeps a song off a record; formula and rhymes
694.s: Hunter rejects generic songs, describes his two-straight-verses-and-a-joke formula, and the cul-de-sac rhyme from 'One Way Love'.
694.q: Oh if it’s a bit too generic. But for shorter stuff I’ll put it in. If it sounds like anyone could have written it, if it really sounds — doesn’t have any distinctive touches or, you know, then I’ll feel like — because sometimes I’ve deliberately tried, just for the sake of writing something, to…

694.s: Hunter talks about the horn lick, the late third verse, and choosing a familiar phrase as the title.
694.q: Oh “You Can’t Win” here we’re going back here aren’t we. Yeah. Yeah that was just tacked on. That wasn’t like really integral. That was just to give the horn players something to do. We’re all here, we might as well do something. You know. That’s why that one didn’t really stick in my mind that…

694.t: Lyric writing and real names in fictional stories
694.s: Hunter says his lyrics come from real life or imagined conversations, with real names and fictitious stories.
694.q: Well real life, either mine or other people’s. You know, or imagined conversations, what I would have said to somebody you know under certain circumstances which haven’t actually happened. So yeah it’s just all observations, some things like that. You know anything that’s all my own half-baked…

544.t: Pitch modules technique from Brookmeyer and Albam
544.s: He studied in the BMI Jazz Composers' Workshop and uses three-note pitch modules to generate melodies and harmonies, as in the Airmen chart.
544.q: Well you know what I did? In 1989 and ’91 I spent two years studying with Bob Brookmeyer and Manny Albam in the BMI Jazz Composers’ Workshop. And they taught us a technique called “Pitch Modules” where you take three note pitch cells and use it to develop raw material from which to write music. And…

544.t: Writing on score paper; Dave Rivello and Sam DeAngelo
544.s: Kirchner cannot write on computer and uses a copyist; he and Dave Rivello both studied arranging with Sam DeAngelo in Youngstown.
544.q: Ut uh. I can’t write on the computer. I still have to write on score paper, and then I have a copyist quote unquote who’s adept on you know Finale and Sibelius who then, I’ll just give the score to and he can load it in for me. I mean I know a number of composers and arrangers who are like me, who…

544.t: Where his musical ideas come from
544.s: He draws on pitch modules, melodies from a person's name, and sometimes pure inspiration, so he is not waiting at the keyboard.
544.q: Well in part from that pitch module process that I told you about, where I just generate some raw material you know to come up with ideas. Other times I’ve written a couple of pieces that were just from a person’s name, you know that you could play the notes on the piano and come up with a melody…

584.t: Art-inspired composing: the Gardner Museum project
584.s: Palmer describes writing a piece for each artwork stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum.
584.q: Yeah, that’s a heavy question. You know I’ve gone through periods where I’ll have several months where I’ll just go and go to a museum, like I went to the Gardner Museum and I just noticed the empty frames. And I said to myself what does that mean? And then I found out what those empty frames in…

584.s: Palmer has never written a wholly through-composed piece; he discusses Jeremy Pelt and a new trio record.
584.q: Yup, yup. Yeah I’ve written some songs where I didn’t have the goal of myself improvising on the song, like I wrote them for other people. I think I first heard that on a Jeremy Pelt record. He recorded a song, I forget the name of it, but he didn’t even solo in the song and I thought oh this is…

584.s: Palmer explains writing from the head, the Tadd Dameron-like motif and the rhythm of the tune in three.
584.q: Yeah I mean, yeah I write everything from up here. I don’t write from an instrument. I mean I’ve written a few tunes from the instrument, from the trumpet or, you know I started playing guitar a little bit. But I’ve never really written a full tune off of the instrument. But I think, but that tune…

524.t: Commissions and how she approaches them
524.s: She dislikes commissions that dictate a feature, needing writing to come from personal feeling, as with the Spartacus arrangement for Toots Thielemans.
524.q: Well the first thing is, actually I don’t like getting commissions. I know every composer likes commissions, because it means you’re being paid to write. But I put myself through a psychological trip a little bit when I get a commission. Luckily people don’t say to me I’d like you to do something…

524.t: Throwing away the jazz grid and composing without bar lines
524.s: She criticizes jazz templates, describes the resources of her orchestra, and her process of dancing, singing and writing on unbarred score paper.
524.q: Yeah. You know it’s something I started to realize about jazz, because I have to say I’m really disappointed in a lot of jazz I hear — not that I listen and say I’m disappointed — but I just lose interest pretty quickly. And I think that jazz at one time was music that, it just evolved. Later it…

524.s: She writes only at score paper and piano, finding synthesizers a distraction though Kenny Werner uses them well.
524.q: Yeah I do all my writing just in front of score paper and then using a piano. I don’t use synthesizers. Some people use it to really develop their ideas. I know Kenny Werner uses things, and he turns things upside down and tries all different combinations of things and he writes beautiful music.…

487.t: How Sheller starts an original piece
487.s: He begins with a rhythm and bass line that imply chords, melody comes later; ideas jotted by his bed after listening to albums.
487.q: Yes. It’ll be either thinking of what rhythm I want to use and then a bass line that implies some chords, and we go from there.

487.t: Reusing sketches, forms and odd meters
487.s: Pasting an old eight-bar idea into a new arrangement, preferred phrase lengths, and a 5/4 piece written for Giovanni Hidalgo.
487.q: Very perceptive. Yes. That is true. Being exactly that situation. I’m usually — I usually don’t have things sitting around, but every now and then there are some things that I’ll start working on and for some reason not get back to it. I’ve got one right now that’s on the keyboard that I’ve got…

487.s: He writes by notes and harmonies and finds titles only at the end; Rowe mentions Bela Fleck's list of titles.
487.q: Good question. I never think of a title before I start to write. I know certain composers will get an idea about I don’t know, look out the window and see a beautiful scene and say that reminds me of the time I went to Acapulco so I’m going to write something that would be appropriate for that. I’m…

501.t: Why he cannot write poetry to jazz
501.s: Jazz and poetry are different; he writes to classical music, not jazz, and reflects on Bach as an improviser.
501.q: It’s a difficult question to answer straight on. The thing is that they are entirely different things. Jazz, as stimulus, jazz has a way of keeping that part of the mind that hooks up the, hooks up reason and intuition which basically is what poetry is. They could work that way as jazz as an…

165.t: Social Call for Ernestine Anderson; writing a song a week

165.t: Building a story from a title: Woodside, Freddie Freeloader, Evidence
165.s: He starts from the title and builds characters and a plot, with examples from Woodside, Freddie Freeloader and Monk's Evidence.

Like the Woodside was a hotel in New York where not only the Basie band, but all the bands – Andy Kirk, Jay McShann, everybody that came to New York, all the bands that came to New York – could check in, get rooms…

165.t: Writing lyrics to Weston, Golson and Gryce tunes; Leonard Feather
165.s: He lists tunes he wrote words for and explains Leonard Feather wrote Whisper Not.

80.t: Composing in his head and hearing tunes by ear

80.t: When Fats put his on-the-spot tunes on paper
80.s: Fats wrote tunes down only when he needed money, for whiskey rather than food, mostly before he had the band.
80.q: When -- that, or when he needed some money. (Laughs.) And after he got started with the band it was very seldom he needed money. This was more or less when he was alone by himself, with -- when he needed -- when he needed that extra buck.

80.s: Autrey says Fats wrote 'Ain't Misbehavin'', 'My Fate Is in Your Hands' and 'Keepin' Out of Mischief Now' while jailed for alimony, with Andy Razaf and J. C. Johnson as lyricists.

677.t: Hodges's obligatos and the song factory
677.s: Hodges' obligatos against Once in a While became Don't Get Around Much Anymore and Don't Let a Song Go Out of My Heart; words came from the office.
677.q: "Don't get around much any more" -- Johnny Hodges. That's another one of the fellows that never received near what he should have.

677.t: Other contributed tunes and Golden Crest
677.s: He cannot name other tunes, played from love of music, and wrote Golden Crest as his own concert piece.
677.q: always running up there, playing some melody or some phrases, and, you know, that was the end of it. We'd just do it out of just love for music. We didn't think too much about commercializing on what we did.

677.t: Reel Five: Tizol's Perdido and Lost in Meditation
677.s: Brown repeats that Tizol hummed Perdido for weeks and notes he rarely soloed apart from his themes.
677.q: Yes, he did, uh-huh. I knew he did cause I had to sit next to him for weeks and weeks in the theaters -- dressing rooms. And he kept drilling at this tune he had in his mind, which was "Perdido."

148.t: The flood of new writing: Gray Suede, Key F and Dalvatore
148.s: Once the block lifted the pieces poured out, and he regrets that others turned them into suites.

148.s: He writes what he hears without a system and is often astonished by the results.

148.t: Programmatic titles and humor and anger in his music
148.s: His titles came with pictured stories, and he finds his music both humorous and angry.

If it was a title it also had a picture or a story in my head, and I would almost tailor-make the music as if I…

95.t: Triumph in London and writing "Woman, Be Wise"
95.s: She was scared but drew huge crowds, and wrote "Woman, Be Wise" on the spot when the show wanted new songs.

95.q: ten, thirteen thousand, twenty-five thousand people, (unintelligible) you could see all the people in the world were there. So then they said to me they had to make new songs. That's why "Woman, Be Wise."

95.t: Writing songs from her own feelings
95.s: She says every song she wrote came from her feelings and that she is only talking about herself.
95.q: Uh-huh, every song I wrote is from my feelings. That's why I say I write about something about -- I'm talking about myself when I write me a song. I'm talking about myself. Can't nobody get mad about what I say because I ain't talking about nobody but myself.

13.t: Writing Blue Because of You, Harlem Lament and Dominick Swing
13.s: Wilson describes composing these tunes and the Dominick of the Harlem gin mill.

13.t: Hampton's record of Blue Because of You
13.q: Only ones they mentioned -- I knew about Earl, we recorded it about two or three different times. Only others I remember was Fats Waller made it. And who else, somebody else made it. I forgot who it was now. I was surprised.

13.t: Charlie Carpenter, lyrics for Blue Because of You, Harlem Lament
13.s: Carpenter and Louis Dunlap wrote words; Wilson explains how he wrote Harlem Lament.
13.q: I don't know whose. Must have been their title, because they wrote the words. I wrote the music, first. I didn't figure on, you know, publishing or nothing like that. I just wrote it for a recording session.

257.t: How he writes tunes at the piano

22.t: Composing as a faker from old chord constructions

979.t: Writing 'A Dog' for her Yorkie FiFi
979.s: She wrote the tune after the dog died, and bandmates at a Town Hall concert struggled with its odd four-four.

979.t: Her composing process and attitude to the present
979.s: Ideas arrive as feeling before she reaches the piano; she feels the world has caught up with her and still writes by pen.

But it’s there before I go to the piano. However, the piano is such a great translator, almost equal to going on- line on the computer.…

1032.t: Where her compositions come from: influences and piano versus horn
1032.s: She is influenced by everything, especially Don Pullen and others, and writes at either piano or horn, much during Covid.
1032.q: Pretty much everything. Just, you know, like I like to paint and it’s the same thing, like when I compose I try and look at it like it’s always like my first piece and my last. Like this…

980.s: Rowe praises titles like Backstabber's Ball and The Hempire Strikes Back; Caine describes his unsystematic approach to writing.

980.s: Players alter his written parts; he picks pretty notes for two tenors and likes tenor players who avoid sounding like Shorter or Coltrane.

And like you know I have a sax player who I love who plays in my band sometimes, Stephen Riley. And I’ll write like a song with the harmony.…

1021.t: How he writes songs and what Nashville taught him
1021.s: He starts from a melody and writes lyrics last; Nashville taught him storytelling in lyrics.
1021.q: Sometimes I’ll get a title maybe or I’ll hear a phrase or something will pop into my head. More often than not I’ll hear some kind of little piece of melody or melody and a couple of changes, and then I’ll try and develop that. And normally the lyric kind of comes last, oddly enough — or maybe not…

1021.s: A clip of his tune 'Country', inspired by the farm road near Prospect, played by friend Mark Hatch.

754.t: Composing by intuition and starting bands to solve musical problems
754.s: Galper says he does not compose deliberately and formed bands to work out concepts such as pentatonics and cells, which took fifteen and ten years.
754.q: I don’t compose deliberately. It has to be an accident. I don’t force it. I love my intuition telling me what to do. If my intuition has a tune it’ll come up. I’ve got a tune I’ve been working on, fragments, gorgeous fragments, I’ve been trying to finish for a couple of years. Last night I was…

599.t: Writing lyrics to Think of One from a limousine job

599.t: Writing lyrics to Milestones for Miles Tones
599.s: His creative process: living with a melody for three months, then writing lyrics in half an hour.

915.s: His writing draws on church music and blues; in college he heard a whole wind-ensemble piece in his head over three days, did not write it down, and lost it; he now writes everything down.
